name: Pink Purple
lede: Pink Purple is a vivid magenta-violet that earns its name from the color-name survey run by the web comic xkcd in 2010, and its value is a screen convention rather than a historical color.

sections.title: A survey name
sections.body:
Pink Purple has no pigment or dye behind it [1]. Our library records it from one source, the xkcd color survey of 2010, in which respondents typed names for colors shown on screen [1]. The survey also produced Purple Pink and Pinkish Purple, which sit within 1.5 and 1.2 units of color difference of this swatch, so the three names describe the same region of color [1]. Its closest named neighbors in the app are [[magenta]], [[orchid]] and [[purple]] [1], with [[violet]] on the bluer side.

The plain name is itself the finding. Westland lists pink and purple among the eleven basic color terms, which he says are widely understood irrespective of culture and language, and calls them more salient than names such as fuchsia [2]. Joining the two words is the survey's own way of naming a color between them.

sections.title: Why it has no spectrum
sections.body:
This color is not found in the rainbow. Eckstut explains that pinks and purples, like grays and dull colors, are nonspectral colors, which are mixtures of wavelengths of light [3]. Magenta, the pink-purple pole, has a story of its own: St Clair notes that it is now considered a pink but was originally closer to a purple-red [4].

Pastoureau adds a related point about fashion: in the sixteenth century, when bright reds fell from favor, people turned to darker shades such as crimson, or to shades only bordering on red, such as pink and purple [5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our archive of 23,781 has this color covering at least 1 per cent of its canvas, within a color difference of 4, as photographed [6]. That describes our archive, not painting as a whole, and a saturated screen-magenta is far brighter than historical pigments and lakes, which fade [6]. In printed English the phrase peaks in the 1980s, and it rose fastest in the 1880s [7]. The Google Books count counts every use of the words, including ordinary descriptions of flowers, so it is a rough guide [7].
